title: Why CXMT’s Memory Expansion Could Reshape the DRAM Market
author: T
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Memory competition could reshape both the cost of computing and the way future processors are designed. Charles Kao’s prediction that CXMT will deliver large volumes of DRAM within two years points to potential pricing pressure around 2028. However, that timeline remains an industry forecast, rather than a guaranteed production outcome.

If CXMT successfully expands output, buyers could gain cheaper memory and greater negotiating power. Established suppliers would face pressure to defend margins, differentiate their products, and reconsider capacity investments. The implications extend beyond semiconductor manufacturers: memory costs influence the economics of PCs, smartphones, servers, and other devices. More supply could ease purchasing costs, although the benefits would depend on product quality, customer qualification, and where those chips can actually be sold.

The TSMC discussion matters for a different reason. Its demonstrated back-end-of-line, or BEOL, memory embeds storage within the interconnect layers of a logic chip. Research presented in 2025 described a solution offering greater density than SRAM, with low power consumption and short access times. That creates a potential route toward fitting more useful memory close to computation.

These developments address different markets and should be judged separately. Expanding conventional DRAM production concerns the supply of memory components. Integrating BEOL memory concerns processor architecture and local storage. TSMC could make progress in the latter without becoming a major supplier of standalone DRAM. Equally, additional conventional memory would not automatically resolve every constraint affecting advanced AI systems.

The broader significance is that competition may intensify along two dimensions: manufacturing scale and technical integration. CXMT could challenge the industry’s pricing structure, while TSMC’s research could change how designers balance memory capacity, energy use, and chip area. For customers, the opportunity is more affordable, efficient computing. The decisive evidence will be commercial yields, reliable products, customer adoption, and delivered costs—not ambitious forecasts or promising laboratory demonstrations alone.
